A model is sloppy, at a parameter point and for a given observation design, when the eigenvalues of its Fisher information, in a declared chart (conventionally the logarithms of its bare parameters), spread over many decades, and no gap among them marks off the combinations that matter from those that do not. The term separates this from four neighbours: ill-conditioning (one ratio, which a single gap can produce), singularity (a zero eigenvalue on a stratum), the hyperribbon (the chart-free shape of the predictions, [TERM-135](../../../record/terms.d/TERM-135.md)), and a power-law spectrum (a sloppy spectrum falls by roughly a constant factor per rank, so it covers decades in proportion to the number of parameters). Its job is to let the record's entries on sloppiness, singular learning and effective dimension say which of these they mean. The source of the concept is Sethna and colleagues: LIT-2977, LIT-3009 and LIT-2994, read on 2026-11-21 (THEORY-2156, THEORY-2155, THEORY-2154), and LIT-2999, unread. They define sloppiness by example and by an eigenvalue spread "roughly evenly spaced" in log, and put its chart-free content in the widths of the model manifold; version 2 records what they say. The wording is the assistant's (Claude, in this session); adopting it is the owner's call. | Proposed |
